performers: Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
question: How does a Requiem open with one chord and no solo voice?
intro: Fauré begins with a single D and a six-part choir that hardly moves from one chord. Follow the prayer as it passes to a tenor melody, a forte plea and a Kyrie that borrows the tenor’s tune.

sections.label: The tenors’ prayer
sections.mNote: tenor melody over violas, cellos, basses and organ

sections.label: Kyrie
sections.mNote: the tenor melody, now in unison for three voices

sections.label: Kyrie · the close
sections.mNote: the Kyrie returns pianissimo and fades away

cues.title: One note, then one chord
cues.text: Bassoons, horns and low strings attack a single D fortissimo and let it fade. The choir enters pianissimo, divided into six parts, and holds a D minor chord under “Requiem aeternam” while the strings sustain beneath. Listen for how little the harmony moves.
cues.evidence: Page 1 of the score gives bassoons, horns, violas, cellos and basses the opening D marked ff to pp, with the choir pp sostenuto over sustained strings. The report’s first windows sit at −30.5 to −17.7 dB with D minor as the local key estimate. Wikipedia’s account of the movement describes the six-part choir on one chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first swell
cues.text: The music swells to the loudest point of this opening paragraph, on “et lux perpetua” (“and perpetual light”), then falls away through “luceat eis” (“let it shine on them”). Hear it as one gesture of the whole choir.
cues.evidence: Relative level climbs from −18.8 dB at 0:30 to −5.0 dB at 0:40, and the report’s strongest boundary is 0:36. The score places the crescendo on “et lux perpetua” at letter A and the diminuendo on “luceat eis”; the report does not time the words.

cues.title: Why a Requiem?
cues.text: Fauré’s father died in 1885 and his mother on New Year’s Eve 1887. Yet he had begun the work before his mother died, and later called it written “for pleasure, if I may call it that”. His reasons remain uncertain.
cues.evidence: The History section of the Wikipedia article on the Requiem gives the 1885 and 1887 deaths, says the work was begun before the second, calls the motive uncertain, and quotes Fauré’s remark. René Gagnaux’s Frémaux page prints the French form of the remark.

cues.title: The pace almost doubles
cues.text: After a held chord the marking changes from Molto largo, quarter note = 40, to Andante moderato, quarter note = 72. The tenors alone take up the prayer over violas, cellos and basses, with the organ entering softly; horns and bassoons fall silent.
cues.evidence: The quietest window in the report is 1:35 (−31.4 dB, brightness 1967 Hz), between louder windows at 1:30 and 1:40. The score shows a fermata at the end of page 4, the new tempo and the organ’s first entry on page 5, and no wind parts on pages 5–9.

cues.title: Where and when it was recorded
cues.text: The record sleeve names Monaco’s cathedral and 11 August 1962; Commons and several listings give 10 August, in the Salle Alcazar. Louis Frémaux conducts the Monte-Carlo orchestra, with Canon Henri Carol at the organ.
cues.evidence: The scanned Erato sleeve (Internet Archive item faure-o-requiem-cantique-de-jean-racine-louis-fremaux) prints the cathedral, the date, the conductor and the organist. Commons, IMSLP and Gagnaux give 10 August 1962 and the Salle Alcazar. The dossier records the date and place as disputed.

cues.title: Winds return, forte
cues.text: Bassoons, horns and trumpets, silent through the tenors’ prayer, return with forte chords marked to diminish at once. The organ adds reed stops to its foundations. A moment later the sopranos begin “Te decet hymnus”, and the orchestra drops to a hush.
cues.evidence: The report shows brightness rising to 1856 Hz and level to −9.5 dB at 2:30, with a boundary at 2:32. Page 10 of the score (letter E) has forte bassoon, horn and trumpet chords marked dim., the organ marked “Anches et fonds”, and no wind staves playing on pages 5–9.

cues.title: Sopranos alone, very quiet
cues.text: Through this stretch the sopranos sing “Te decet hymnus” (“praise is due to you”) and “et tibi reddetur votum” (“and the vow shall be paid to you”) over gently moving violas and cellos. Bassoons and horns join pianissimo at the end of the phrase.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls to −20.9 dB at 2:55, −24.7 dB at 3:00 and −22.0 dB at 3:05, the quietest sustained stretch after the tenors’ prayer. Pages 11–12 of the score give the soprano line, the viola and cello figures and the bassoon and horn chords.

cues.title: Exaudi, fortissimo
cues.text: At letter F every voice sings “exaudi” (“hear”) fortissimo against forceful strings. It is the movement’s strongest choral plea, and the prayer turns from consoling to insistent. The loud stretch continues through “ad te omnis caro veniet”.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −14.0 dB at 3:30 to −6.4 dB at 3:35, then reaches −6.0 dB at 3:50 and −7.3 dB at 3:55; the report places a boundary at 3:34. The score marks ff for the choir at letter F on page 13 and the text “ad te omnis caro veniet” on pages 14–15.

cues.title: The Kyrie borrows the tenor tune
cues.text: The Kyrie begins with the tenors’ earlier melody, now sung in unison by sopranos, altos and tenors, then repeated in four-part harmony. A prayer first given to one voice is shared by the choir.
cues.evidence: The report finds a boundary at 4:10 and a drop to −17.3 dB after the loud “Exaudi” passage. Wikipedia’s description of the movement and page 16 of the score give the unison opening of the Kyrie on the tenor melody; the report does not measure the repeat.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Christe, urgent then softer
cues.text: The call of “Christe” is strong and urgent the first time, then repeated more softly while the violas and cellos keep moving beneath it. Bassoons, horns and trumpets add pianissimo chords in the later “Christe” bars.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −16.5 dB at 4:35 to −7.6 dB at 4:40, reaches −8.3 dB at 4:45 and −8.4 dB at 4:55, and falls to −17.6 dB at 5:10. Pages 17–19 of the score mark the crescendo to “Christe” and show the bassoon, horn and trumpet chords marked pp.

cues.title: Too many novelties
cues.text: After the 1888 funeral service at the Madeleine, the priest is reported to have summoned Fauré and told him: “We don’t need all these novelties: the Madeleine’s repertoire is quite rich enough.”
cues.evidence: A note in the Versions section of the Wikipedia article on the Requiem reports the priest’s remark, citing Jessica Duchen’s biography Gabriel Fauré (Phaidon, 2000), page 80. The anecdote is secondary reporting and the wording is as printed there.

cues.title: The sound drains away
cues.text: In the last page the choir’s pianissimo “eleison” settles over strings and organ, and the sound thins out. Listen to the file’s final seconds as the level falls towards silence, with the strings marked “sempre al fine”.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −21.9 dB at 6:00 to −28.4 dB at 6:15 and −43.2 dB at 6:20, with a boundary at 6:08. The cello and bass parts on pages 21–22 are marked pp sempre al fine.

transitions.title: A held chord, then one voice
transitions.how: The six-part choir ends its first paragraph pianissimo on a fermata. Fauré then changes almost everything at once: Molto largo (quarter note = 40) gives way to Andante moderato (quarter note = 72), the bassoons and horns fall silent, and the organ enters for the first time with soft foundation stops. A single tenor line takes the prayer over violas, cellos and basses. The words are the same; the choir’s dense chord becomes a melody that moves.
transitions.evidence: The quietest window in the report is 1:35 (−31.4 dB, brightness 1967 Hz), between louder windows at 1:30 and 1:40, which fits a held chord and a pause before the new tempo. The score marks the fermata at the end of page 4, the new tempo and the organ’s “Fonds de 8 p.” on page 5, and no wind parts on pages 5–9. Machine key estimates are not used.

transitions.title: Horns and bassoons break the quiet
transitions.how: After a long stretch without wind instruments, bassoons, horns and trumpets enter at letter E with forte chords marked to diminish at once. The organ adds reed stops to its foundations (“anches et fonds”) and the strings sustain under the chords. The sopranos then take up the next words, “Te decet hymnus”, with the orchestra lowered to a hush. The join is a flash of colour between two quiet textures, not a change of tempo.
transitions.evidence: The report shows brightness rising to 1856 Hz and level to −9.5 dB at 2:30, with a boundary at 2:32. Page 10 of the score (letter E) has forte bassoon and horn chords marked dim. and the organ marked “Anches et fonds”; pages 5–9 have no wind parts. The timing describes the whole join, not a bar.

transitions.title: From a hush to “Exaudi”
transitions.how: The sopranos’ quiet “Te decet hymnus” is carried by gently moving violas and cellos. As the next line of text begins, the strings crescendo and the voices gather, and at letter F the whole choir sings “exaudi” fortissimo against marked strings, with bassoons, horns and trumpets adding soft chords above. Fauré moves from consolation to insistence by dynamics and texture alone: the same prayer is now declaimed instead of murmured.
transitions.evidence: Relative level rises from −14.0 dB at 3:30 to −6.4 dB at 3:35, with a boundary at 3:34. The score marks a crescendo at the end of page 12 and ff for the choir and strings at letter F on page 13; the report does not separate the instruments.

transitions.title: The tenor tune returns as a Kyrie
transitions.how: “Ad te omnis caro veniet” (“to you all flesh shall come”) falls from forte to pianissimo at letter G, with bassoons, horns and trumpets answering dolce. The Greek text then begins on the tenors’ earlier melody, now in unison for sopranos, altos and tenors and repeated in four-part harmony. The recall connects the Kyrie to the Introit: a new text begins on a familiar shape.
transitions.evidence: The report shows a boundary at 4:10 and level falling to −17.3 dB after the loud stretch at 3:50–4:05. Pages 15–16 of the score mark the diminuendo at G and the unison Kyrie; the identity with the tenor melody comes from the written form (Wikipedia’s account of the movement), not from a measured match.

transitions.title: The Kyrie builds into an urgent Christe
transitions.how: The Kyrie’s unison phrases swell at letter H while violas, cellos and basses cut across them with rising and falling lines. The text then changes to “Christe”, which Fauré marks strong and urgent at its first statement, with the strings at fortissimo. Later repetitions are softer, and bassoons, horns and trumpets add pianissimo chords. The change of text is signalled by louder strings and a new, more broken choral rhythm.
transitions.evidence: Relative level rises from −16.5 dB at 4:35 to −7.6 dB at 4:40 and reaches −8.3 dB at 4:45. The score marks cresc. at letter H (page 17) and ff strings with the Christe text on page 18; the wind and trumpet chords appear on pages 18–19.

transitions.title: Christe falls away into the last Kyrie
transitions.how: The cries of “Christe” fall to pianissimo by letter J and the choir returns to “Kyrie eleison” in short quiet phrases. Beneath them the cellos and basses keep moving while the violas sustain, marked “sempre al fine”. Near letter K a bassoon and a horn each sing a dolce line over the choir. The movement ends without a climax, in the unhurried speech that opened the Kyrie.
transitions.evidence: Relative level falls from −10.8 dB at 5:05 to −17.6 dB at 5:10, with boundaries at 5:24 and 6:08. Pages 19–22 of the score show the diminuendo, the strings marked pp sempre al fine, and the dolce bassoon and horn lines at letter K.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: I. Introït et Kyrie, printed pp. 1–22. The violin, flute, clarinet, trombone, timpani and harp staves are empty throughout. Entries are set at section boundaries taken from the report, so an instrument that plays in only part of a span is listed for the whole span.

timeline.note: Bassoons, horns and low strings hold a D that fades; the six-part choir enters pianissimo. The organ and violins are silent.
The tenors sing over violas, cellos and basses, with the organ’s foundation stops entering for the first time.
Bassoons, horns and trumpets return with forte chords marked to diminish.
The sopranos sing “Te decet hymnus” over violas and cellos, with bassoons and horns joining pianissimo at the end of the phrase.
The full choir sings “exaudi” fortissimo over forceful strings; bassoons, horns and trumpets add soft chords above.
The last held wind chords fade as the Kyrie opens in unison on the tenor melody.
The winds rest through the Kyrie’s unison and four-part phrases.
Bassoons, horns and trumpets add pianissimo chords under the “Christe” calls.
The final Kyrie is sung pianissimo over moving cellos and basses and sustained violas.
A bassoon and a horn each add a dolce line over the choir’s last phrases before the sound fades.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Chorale Philippe Caillard (chorus), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ)
fields.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; neither has a solo part in this movement. The organist is named on the sleeve (“Chanoine Henri Carol”), not on Commons.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
fields.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
fields.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.
alts: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Commons names “Erato Records” as source; the sleeve, BnF and Discogs give the Erato label.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.44 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 1, track 1 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+40 cents (CQT histogram) and +0.48 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning)); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in jurisdictions applying an unextended life-plus-70-year term
fields.note: Gabriel Fauré died in 1924. This assessment concerns the original composition, not a later edition, arrangement or this recording; it is not a worldwide rights clearance.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
fields.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

composer.epithet: A church organist who made the French song and the chamber ensemble laboratories for harmony.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; piano with Camille Saint-Saëns
Madeleine: choirmaster 1877–96, organist 1896–1905 · Paris Conservatoire: composition professor 1896–1905, director 1905–20
Mélodies, piano music, chamber music, Requiem, the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
Fauré learned his trade in a school for church musicians. His father was a schoolmaster in the Ariège; at nine, Gabriel was sent to Louis Niedermeyer’s recently founded school in Paris, where plainchant, Renaissance polyphony, organ playing and counterpoint belonged to the ordinary curriculum. The education matters to the harmony. A melody can cadence in minor with an unsharpened seventh degree; a chord can emerge from the independent movement of voices. These possibilities were practical knowledge before they became a recognisable Fauré style.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class and introduced the pupils to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner. Teacher and pupil remained friends for more than sixty years. Fauré’s graduation work, the Cantique de Jean Racine of 1865, already joins the two educations: a flowing keyboard accompaniment beneath a choral texture whose entries are controlled by contrapuntal discipline. Its French text is Racine’s paraphrase of a Latin hymn. The bass supports long phrases that carry the upper voices across the bar-lines.
